stirs up the fire, so that both the <term>catinus</term> <gloss>receiving pit</gloss> and the <term>focus</term> <gloss>hearth</gloss> are sufficiently heated within the space of half an hour. Indeed, they heat up more quickly if ore was smelted in the same furnace the previous day, and more slowly if it was not. If the hearth and pit are not heated before the ore to be smelted is thrown in, they will be damaged and the metals will be lost. For if the powder from which both are made is damp in the summer or frozen in the winter, both will burst apart along with the metals and other materials, making a sound like thunder and scattering everywhere, not without great danger to the men.

Then the master should throw <term>recrementa</term> <gloss>slag</gloss> into the furnace; when these have liquefied, they flow out from the mouth into the pit. Soon he blocks the mouth with clay mixed with charcoal dust; he applies this by hand with a rounded wooden <term>pilum</term> <gloss>pestle</gloss> that is five fingers thick and two palms high, with a handle three feet long. Then he extracts the slag from the pit with a hooked pole. If he is about to smelt rich ore of gold or silver, he places a hundred-weight of lead into the pit; if it is poor ore, half that amount. For he has need of much lead for the former, and little for the latter. 

Soon he should throw firebrands over the lead so that it melts; afterwards he performs everything in due order, throwing materials into the furnace in a specific sequence. First, he adds as much of the cakes melted from <term>pyrite</term> <gloss>sulfide minerals</gloss> as is needed to smelt the ore. Next, he adds as much as two troughs can hold of ore mixed with <term>spuma argenti</term> <gloss>litharge</gloss> and <term>molybdæna</term> <gloss>galena</gloss>, along with stones of the second kind that melt easily in the fire. Then he adds as many coals as a trough woven of wooden strips can hold; finally, more slag. Once the furnace is filled with these stated things, he smelts the ore little by little. He must not throw the ore too close to the back wall of the furnace, lest it become <term>ferruminata</term> <gloss>sintered or frozen</gloss> around the <term>nares</term> <gloss>nozzles</gloss> of the bellows, which would impede the blast and cause the fire to burn less brightly.

Indeed, that man has always been counted among the excellent smelters who can properly temper the four elements. He tempers them who throws no more than is fitting into the furnace of the ore, which partakes of earth; who pours in water whenever the matter requires it; who moderates the blast of the bellows with skill; and who casts the ore into the fire where it burns most brightly. The master should moisten the charcoal by gradually pouring water into both sides of the furnace, so that the finest particles of the ores stick to them; otherwise, these particles would be agitated and lifted up by the blast of the bellows and the force of the fires, flying away with the smoke.

But because the nature of the ores to be smelted is diverse, smelters find it necessary to prepare the hearth sometimes high and sometimes low, and to place the pipe in which the nozzles of the bellows are situated sometimes at a very steep angle and sometimes at a shallow one. They must also inspire the furnace with a blast from the bellows that is sometimes gentle and sometimes vehement. For ores that heat and melt quickly, the smelters need a low hearth, a pipe placed with a shallow incline, and a gentle blast of the bellows. Conversely, for those that heat and melt slowly, they need a high hearth, a pipe positioned with a steep incline, and a vehement blast. For these slower ores, they also need a very hot furnace in which slag has previously been re-smelted, or cakes melted from pyrite, or stones that melt easily in the fire. Unless these things are done, the ores settling in the hearth of the furnace block the mouth and, as it were, suffocate it; this is also often caused by the tiny metallic particles that settled while the ores were being washed. Furthermore, large bellows should have wide nozzles; for if they are narrow, a great and powerful blast is forced into the furnace too tightly and sharply. <summary>This page details the technical procedures for preparing and operating a smelting furnace, focusing on preheating the hearth and the precise sequence of adding lead, fluxes, and ore. It explains how a master smelter must balance the four elements through moisture, airflow, and temperature to prevent ore loss and equipment damage.</summary>
